pages.title: Modi on Russia as India's best friend
pages.summary: Modi's words at the BRICS summits call Russia India's best friend and pillar of development and security, and he says one old friend is better than two new ones. Russia's 2016 foreign policy concept affirms a special privileged partnership with India, and Modi was invited to the St Petersburg Economic Forum in June 2017.

pages.title: Sibal and KC Singh views; strategic partnership status
pages.summary: Kanwal Sibal sees a definite decline despite the rhetoric, while KC Singh calls for deft balancing. Russia was India's first strategic partner (2000), upgraded in 2010 to a special and privileged partnership, with annual summits and meetings at SCO, BRICS and the East Asia Summit.

pages.title: Annual dialogues; relations lost Indo-Soviet intensity
pages.summary: Foreign and defence ministers hold annual dialogues under intergovernmental commissions. Sibal says the biggest problem is that there has been no serious problem, causing complacency, and C. Raja Mohan hopes Russia's drift toward China and Pakistan will bring realism to India.

pages.title: More problems: government-only ties, generations, connectivity
pages.summary: Russia depends more on China and Pakistan geographically, India-Russia ties remain government-to-government, and new generations lack Cold War memory. Connectivity raises transport costs until the International North South Transport Corridor is fully operational.

pages.title: Early history and Indo-Soviet Phase I (to 1953)
pages.summary: Links date back to Nikitin's visit and Gujarati merchants in Astrakhan, with Russia the first home of Indology and the Great Game against Britain. In Phase I, Russia recognised Indian independence but Stalin criticised non-alignment and called Nehru a bourgeois compradore after India joined the Commonwealth.

pages.title: Khrushchev phase, Tashkent and the 1971 treaty
pages.summary: In Phase II (1953-70) Khrushchev visited India, the Sino-Soviet rift made India a balancer, and the USSR helped with industry, science and defence while also courting Pakistan; the 1965 Tashkent agreement was not in India's favour. Phase III (1971-91), the golden period, began with the Treaty of Peace and Friendship, a quasi alliance.

pages.title: Article 9, Cold War features, 1991-93 strain
pages.summary: Article 9 was a mutual security guarantee, and a USSR-India-Vietnam axis formed, with Soviet defence supply, barter trade, technology transfer and steady support on Kashmir. In 1991-93 Yeltsin's pro-west Russia pressed India on NPT and demanded debt payment in dollars.

pages.title: Yeltsin's repair, Putin's partnership, defence concerns
pages.summary: After denying cryogenic technology, Yeltsin visited in 1993 and renegotiated the treaty without a mutual security clause, Primakov proposed the Russia-India-China triangle and Putin created the strategic partnership. Russia's defence monopoly is declining as India-USA defence trade reaches about 18 billion dollars.

pages.title: Defence grievances on both sides
pages.summary: Russia says Indian defence tenders are not transparent, while India cites cost escalation, delays, poor servicing and missing spare parts, plus Russian sales of Sukhoi 35 and submarines to China and Mi-35 helicopters to Pakistan. Defence nonetheless remains one of the strongest pillars of the partnership.

pages.title: 1977 agreement, co-production and acquired hardware
pages.summary: The 1977 agreement covered equipment export, technology transfer and joint development and marketing. Co-produced items include BrahMos, a 5th generation aircraft, the T-90 tank and Kamov helicopters, and India has acquired INS Vikramaditya and the S-400, but military-to-military exchanges are very limited.

pages.title: Russia-Pakistan military pact and energy partnership
pages.summary: Russia has a comprehensive military agreement with Pakistan, with exercises in 2016 and another due in 2017. On energy, Russia's large reserves attract India but geography limits feasibility, Russia-China pipelines advance, Indian firms lost Sakhalin II, and Russia is building a Karachi-Lahore pipeline.

pages.title: Nuclear and economic partnership
pages.summary: Russia is expected to build 12 new reactors, with Kudankulam phases 5 and 6 agreed, joint uranium mining and cooperation on waste and safety. Economic ties are called the most disappointing aspect, with trade near 11 billion dollars against over 100 billion for Russia-China and India-US.

pages.title: People contact and Russia-China relations
pages.summary: Transportation cost and weak people-to-people contact are listed as weaknesses. Russia-China ties involve competing Siberian claims and Central Asia tension, yet western isolation made Russia the junior partner, and the tactical alliance may soon turn strategic.

pages.title: Russia-Pakistan relations: Bremmer, Korybko, motives
pages.summary: Ian Bremmer calls Pakistan a pivot state and Andrew Korybko calls it a zipper state of Eurasian integration. Russia seeks new friends, markets and security against extremism, while Pakistan gains defence technology, a Russia card against the USA and a way to weaken India's confidence.

pages.title: India's response: old friend and red lines
pages.summary: India can say one old friend is better than two new ones, remind Russia of Pakistan's role in the Soviet collapse and draw a red line on its security. The notes conclude that Russia is more isolated than India and that the two are natural partners.

flashcards.front: How and when did the India-Russia strategic partnership begin, and what is its current status?
flashcards.back: Russia was the first country with which India set up a strategic partnership, on Putin's initiative in 2000. It was raised in 2010 to a special and privileged strategic partnership, which India has only with South Korea, Japan and Russia.

flashcards.front: Besides lack of realism, which structural problems limit India-Russia relations?
flashcards.back: Geography blocks direct energy trade without China or Pakistan, and Russia depends more on them. Ties are government-to-government with little people-to-people contact, new generations lack Cold War memory, and poor connectivity raises transport costs until the International North South Transport Corridor is operational.

flashcards.front: What did Article 9 of the 1971 India-USSR Treaty of Peace and Friendship provide?
flashcards.back: Article 9 was a mutual security guarantee: both parties had to inform each other early of any friction with another country and take all necessary steps to remove the fear and ensure regional security. The treaty was a quasi alliance that gave India the confidence to intervene in East Pakistan.

flashcards.front: Why did India-Russia relations deteriorate in 1991-93, and how were they repaired?
flashcards.back: Yeltsin's Russia and foreign minister Kozyrev turned pro-west, pressed India to sign NPT, demanded debt payment in dollars and denied cryogenic engines. Yeltsin's 1993 visit resolved these issues and renegotiated the treaty, without a mutual security clause.

flashcards.front: What grievances does India hold against Russia in defence cooperation?
flashcards.back: India cites cost escalations, delayed delivery, poor servicing and failure to supply spare parts. New grievances are Russia ending its moratorium on offensive arms sales to China (Sukhoi 35, Amur-class submarines) and giving Pakistan four Mi-35 attack helicopters.

flashcards.front: What features did the 1977 India-Russia defence agreement have, and which items are co-produced?
flashcards.back: It covered export of equipment, transfer of technology, and joint development, marketing and sale. Co-produced items include versions of BrahMos, a 5th generation aircraft, the T-90 tank and Kamov helicopters.

flashcards.front: Why is the India-Russia energy partnership attractive in theory but limited in practice?
flashcards.back: Russia has the largest natural gas reserves, 2nd largest coal and 10th largest oil reserves, but geography limits feasibility. Russia-China pipelines are being built, Indian firms lost Sakhalin II and Sakhalin I is unattractive, so India is seeking Sakhalin III and the Yamal gas field.

flashcards.front: How does India-Russia trade compare with Russia-China and India-US trade, and what problems does the list give?
flashcards.back: India-Russia trade is around 11 billion dollars, against over 100 billion for Russia-China and for India-US. Problems include poor law and order, weak banking infrastructure, protectionism, strict visas, Russia's tensions with the west, India's trade with the west and transportation cost.

flashcards.front: How do the notes describe Russia-China relations, and what pushed them closer?
flashcards.back: Relations were not always peaceful, with competing Siberian claims and Russian unease about China in Central Asia. Western policies of isolating Russia pushed it toward China, making Russia the junior partner, and the tactical alliance may soon become strategic.

flashcards.front: How do Ian Bremmer and Andrew Korybko describe Pakistan, and why is Pakistan courting Russia?
flashcards.back: Bremmer calls Pakistan the pivot state of international politics and Korybko calls it the zipper state of Eurasian integration. Pakistan gains high-technology defence equipment and a Russia card against the USA, and it weakens India's confidence in its only all-weather friend.

answers.question: India-Russia relations remain close in rhetoric but have lost the intensity of the Indo-Soviet era. Examine the structural problems and suggest how the partnership can be revived.
answers.intro: India and Russia hold a special and privileged strategic partnership with annual summits, and Modi calls Russia India's best friend. Yet Kanwal Sibal notes a definite decline, and the notes point to structural limits in trade, defence and geography.
body: Complacency: Sibal says the biggest problem is that there has been no serious problem, so both sides grew complacent, while C. Raja Mohan hopes Russia's drift toward China and Pakistan will break India's inertia.

Structural limits: geography blocks direct energy trade without China or Pakistan, ties remain government-to-government, new generations lack Cold War memory, and connectivity costs persist until the International North South Transport Corridor works.
Economic gap: trade is about 11 billion dollars against over 100 billion for Russia-China and India-US, held back by protectionism, weak banking, visa rules and transport costs.

Defence erosion: Russia's monopoly is declining as India turns to the USA and Israel, India cites cost escalation and delays, and Russia sells Sukhoi 35 aircraft to China and Mi-35 helicopters to Pakistan.
Anchors remain: BrahMos, T-90 and Kamov co-production, Kudankulam 5 and 6 and joint uranium mining; KC Singh advises deft balancing rather than opportunistic praise of any leader.
answers.conclusion: The partnership has depth but has lost momentum. Reviving it needs realism, people-to-people links, better connectivity, trade growth and continued co-production in defence and nuclear energy, while India balances its other partners without melodrama.

answers.question: Russia's growing closeness to China and Pakistan challenges India's strategic interests. Analyse the drivers and suggest how India should respond.
answers.intro: Western isolation has pushed Russia toward China while Russia also courts Pakistan through military ties and energy projects. For India, once Russia's closest friend, this threatens a long-trusted balance and demands a calm, realistic response.
body: Russia-China: ties were not always peaceful, with rival Siberian claims and unease about China in Central Asia, but western isolation made Russia the junior partner. The alliance is tactical now and may turn strategic, and Russia has sold Sukhoi 35 aircraft and Amur-class submarines to China.

Russia-Pakistan: Ian Bremmer calls Pakistan a pivot state and Andrew Korybko a zipper state of Eurasian integration. Russia seeks friends, markets and security against extremism, has signed a military agreement, held exercises and is building a Karachi-Lahore pipeline.
Pakistan's motives: high-technology defence equipment, a Russia card against the USA, and weakening India's confidence in its only all-weather friend.

India's response: say one old friend is better than two new ones, remind Russia of Pakistan's role in the Soviet collapse, draw a red line on India's security, and follow KC Singh's deft balancing, since Russia is more isolated than India and the two are natural partners.
answers.conclusion: Russia's moves are driven by isolation more than by hostility to India. India should voice its concerns firmly, keep defence and nuclear cooperation strong, and recognise that a stronger Russia remains beneficial to Indian interests.
